description: If light has no mass then why does it still bend? That was the question that brought this team together years ago. And ever since, we’ve been chasing questions that turn curiosity into real world ideas, from UV solar panels to using sound waves to protect crops from insects. Now, we’re taking that same curiosity here.
summary:
NASA’s SPHEREx mission maps the whole sky in 102 infrared bands, producing far more data than any one person can examine. Objects such as comets, asteroids, brown dwarfs and nearby stars reveal themselves by shifting position between images, and volunteers have found many of them this way. We built SPHEREx Blink so anyone can do this without special software.

A user enters RA and Dec, either in degrees or in the sexagesimal format used by the challenge (for example 08h55m10.831s). The tool finds every SPHEREx image covering that patch through NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive. It aligns them on one sky grid and plays them in time order like a short video, so moving objects stand out against fixed stars. Options include field of view, detector choice, a shared brightness scale for variable stars, and a difference view that highlights change. Each frame shows its date, wavelength and quality flags. Results expire from the cache, so new data releases appear automatically, and views can be shared by URL.

By lowering the barrier to entry, the tool lets more people help find nearby objects in a unique dataset.
details:
SPHEREx Blink is a web tool that turns SPHEREx sky images into a short video. You enter a sky position (RA and Dec), and it finds the images from NASA’s IRSA archive, aligns them, and plays them in time order so moving objects stand out. Options include a difference view, shared brightness scale, field of view, and shareable URLs. New data appears automatically as cached results expire.

It aims to help more people spot comets, asteroids and brown dwarfs, as volunteers have done before. We used Python, FastAPI, Astropy and reproject, with code written with help from Claude. We designed around the different wavelengths in each image, fast-moving stars, and slow downloads. Tests so far use synthetic data. Live testing on all five targets is still to be confirmed.
